descriptions.text: The Floor Protocol ERC1967Proxy contract exposed an unprotected extMulticall function that allowed any external caller to batch-execute arbitrary low-level calls using the proxy's identity. Because the victim had previously approved the proxy to transfer their NFTs, the attacker leveraged extMulticall to enumerate all PPG tokens held by the victim and construct a batch of safeTransferFrom calls routing every token to the attacker's address — no ownership check or caller restriction existed on the multicall entry-point. Vulnerable code snippet: Attack Tx: 0xec8f6d8e114caf8425736e0a3d5be2f93bbea6c01a50a7eeb3d61d2634927b40 Analysis: Floor Protocol exploited — Bored Apes and Pudgy Penguins gone

Attackers exploited the vulnerability by calling the multicall function in the Forwarder contract, altering the last 20 bytes of calldata to the attacker’s address to execute the attack. Vulnerable code snippet: Attack tx: https://explorer.phalcon.xyz/tx/eth/0xec8f6d8e114caf8425736e0a3d5be2f93bbea6c01a50a7eeb3d61d2634927b40 Analysis: https://medium.com/@Jingkangchua/vulnerability-analysis-erc2771-multicall-545cad1f9028 https://blog.verichains.io/p/address-spoofing-attack-the-combination Solution 1. Use the latest version with the vulnerability fixed. OpenZeppelin’s new version of Multicall includes the context suffix length for ERC2771 context data, identifying the expected context suffix length for ERC-2771.

On December 17th, according to SlowMist Cos, Flooring Protocol may have been subjected to a hacker attack, and users are advised to promptly revoke contract authorizations. In a tweet on December 17th, Flooring Protocol announced that "We have determined the cause of exploit to be linked to FP's peripheral/multi-call contract. The team has deployed a fix 2 hours ago, patching the issue. While we continue to investigate and monitor, rest assured that the main contract is safe. Assets in vaults and safeboxes are not affected."

Flooring Protocol on Ethereum was exploited on December 17, 2023 via its peripheral/multicall contract, enabling attackers to mint excessive fpToken balances and redeem them for high-value NFTs worth ~$1.6 million. No chain attack transactions or confirmed vulnerable contract code are publicly available; the mechanism and impact are established from secondary technical sources, with main vault assets reportedly unaffected. An access control flaw in the peripheral/multicall contract permitted arbitrary external calls and bypassed ownership/accounting checks, allowing attackers to mint unbacked fpTokens redeemable for locked NFTs. No publicly confirmed vulnerable implementation exists.
